name: Phosphatidylserine
lead: Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a glycerophospholipid found in all cell membranes, most abundant in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane and enriched in the brain, where it makes up roughly 13 to 15 percent of cortical phospholipids. [2] It is also sold as an oral dietary supplement, usually derived from soy lecithin, marketed for memory and cognition, and in sports and recovery products for exercise stress. [2][1]

In 2003 the US FDA allowed a qualified health claim for PS and cognitive decline, noting the supporting research was limited and preliminary, while the European Food Safety Authority in 2010 concluded that cause and effect had not been established for several PS claims. [2] Clinical trials have studied PS in older adults, children with ADHD and athletes. [3][4][5][6][7] Its role in appearance is indirect: forum discussion presents it as a cortisol-lowering recovery supplement, a claim for which no appearance-focused studies exist.
infobox: Soy lecithin, fish, meat, organ tissue [2]
About 130 mg per day in a Western diet (estimate) [2]

paras: PS has two fatty acids esterified to glycerol and a phosphoserine head group. Plant- and animal-derived PS differ in fatty acid composition. In mammals it is made in the endoplasmic reticulum by head-group exchange from phosphatidylethanolamine or phosphatidylcholine. [2]

Inside cells PS provides docking sites for signalling proteins such as Akt and protein kinase C, associated with neuronal survival and synapse formation. During apoptosis PS flips to the outer membrane and acts as an "eat-me" signal for phagocytes, which is the basis of the widely used annexin V assay. [2][8][9]

Meat and fish are the main dietary sources, with soy lecithin and white beans among plant sources. [2] Early supplements were extracted from bovine brain; concerns about bovine spongiform encephalopathy in the 1990s moved manufacturers to soy-derived PS. [2]

A 2001 trial of soy-derived PS in elderly people with age-associated memory impairment found no significant effect on cognitive performance, and EFSA in 2010 reasoned that bovine and soy PS may differ biologically so results should not be generalised. [2] Later reviews, according to Wikipedia, suggest a possible benefit in mild cognitive impairment, though the mechanism is unclear and the sourcing for that statement is described as needing verification. [2]
No study has examined PS for facial appearance, body composition or other looksmaxxing outcomes.

A 2002 safety report judged a daily regimen in elderly people to be safe, and the FDA's qualified health claim applies to soy-derived products. [2] Supplement labels warn consumers about product-specific issues such as not ingesting included desiccant packets. [10]
No forum threads about PS were available for this entry. It is placed in the recovery category because supplement marketing links it to stress, sleep and workout recovery.

Registered and published human studies of PS cover cognition in healthy children aged 8 to 12 (208 participants), ADHD in children (including a trial combining PS with omega-3 fatty acids), mild cognitive impairment, cognition in older adults, familial dysautonomia, cycling time-trial performance and eSports performance. [3][4][5][6][7][11][12] Results for several of these registrations are not summarised in the registry records used here, and none addresses appearance.

card.summary: Membrane phospholipid sold as a memory and recovery supplement; trials are mainly in cognition, none for appearance.
card.note: FDA health claim is qualified as limited and preliminary; EFSA found no established cause and effect.

quick.overview:
Phosphatidylserine is a fat-like molecule found in every cell membrane and concentrated in the brain. Supplements, now usually soy-derived, are sold for memory and recovery.

Human trials have mostly looked at cognition in older adults, children and athletes. None examine appearance outcomes, so its looksmaxxing role rests on supplement marketing.
quick.mechanism: PS helps anchor signalling proteins in neuron membranes and tags dying cells for removal by immune cells. How oral supplements might affect brain function is not settled.
quick.risks: A 2002 safety report found a daily regimen safe in elderly people. Supplements are unregulated products, and the FDA's 2003 health claim carries a disclaimer that the evidence is limited.
